record.question:
A public web application runs behind an ALB and serves static objects from S3. It is experiencing SQL injection attempts, HTTP floods, and abusive bots. The company wants managed request filtering, enhanced DDoS protection for its public entry points, and controls that prevent users from bypassing those entry points to reach the origins directly.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the application in a second Region and use Route 53 failover routing. Keep the existing public ALB and S3 access paths without request inspection.
Add network ACL rules that deny the source IP addresses observed in recent attacks. Keep S3 publicly readable so legitimate users can bypass blocked paths.

Place CloudFront in front of the ALB and a private S3 origin. Apply WAF SQL injection, rate-based, and appropriate bot rules, enroll eligible public resources in Shield Advanced, use S3 origin access control, and restrict ALB access to the intended CloudFront path.
Place CloudFront in front of both origins and restrict origin access. Enroll the public resources in Shield Advanced, but omit WAF request-inspection rules for SQL injection and bots.

explanation.text:
<<3>> is correct. WAF can inspect HTTP request contents and rates at CloudFront or an ALB. SQL injection rules address payload patterns, and rate-based and bot controls address abusive request behavior. Shield Advanced adds DDoS protections for enrolled eligible resources. CloudFront origin access control and an appropriately restricted S3 bucket policy prevent public S3 bypass, while the ALB needs its own origin-access restriction.

<<1>> adds recovery capacity but does not filter the attack traffic or close direct-origin paths.

<<2>> relies on a changing IP list and network-layer matching rather than inspecting application requests. It also deliberately retains a bypass path.

<<4>> addresses origin bypass and DDoS protection but omits the requested application-specific SQL injection and bot filtering. DDoS protection alone is not an application input-validation policy.

Test and tune WAF rules against legitimate traffic, retain application-side validation, and protect every reachable origin. WAF does not attach directly to an S3 bucket.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [AWS WAF protected resources](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-chapter.html); [WAF SQL injection matching](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rule-statement-type-sqli-match.html); [WAF rate limiting and Bot Control](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/waf-rate-limiting-options.html); [Shield Advanced overview](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-advanced-summary.html); [CloudFront origin access control](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html).

diagram_alt: WAF inspects the public CloudFront path, Shield Advanced protects enrolled entry points, and origin controls reject bypass attempts.

sources.supports: WAF inspects HTTP requests for CloudFront and ALB resources, but does not attach directly to an S3 bucket.
SQL injection statements inspect selected web-request components for malicious SQL patterns.
Rate-based rules and targeted Bot Control offer different configurable mechanisms for web-request rate mitigation.
Shield Advanced expands DDoS protection for enrolled resources and complements WAF protections.
OAC signs CloudFront requests to a regular private S3 origin, with bucket policies restricting access to the intended distribution.

editorial_notes: Preserved answer 3. Added the enhanced-DDoS and origin-bypass requirements to justify the full design. Replaced the unrelated Direct Connect distractor with a realistic design missing application inspection.
